{"id": "7:8/q18", "question": "What events or agents are reported at the balance?", "turns_on": "The differing transmitted descriptions of the balance's location, supervision, announcement, and human experience.", "positions": [{"id": "7:8/q18/p1", "position": "Gabriel oversees the balance and settles claims between people by transfer of good or bad deeds.", "reasons": "Hudhayfa's report in Tabari, Tha'labi, Ibn Atiyya, and al-Durr says good deeds pass from oppressor to victim; if exhausted, the victim's sins pass to the oppressor, leaving a mountain-like burden."}, {"id": "7:8/q18/p2", "position": "A caller or angel announces each person's lasting happiness or misery when the balance tips.", "reasons": "Abd Allah ibn al-Ayzar and Anas supply variant transmitters for the announcement."}, {"id": "7:8/q18/p3", "position": "At the balance people are too preoccupied to recognize or remember others.", "reasons": "Hasan's report through Aisha cites 80:37; Aisha and Qatada place the same distraction also at scattering records and the bridge, with 69:19 cited for books."}, {"id": "7:8/q18/p4", "position": "The balance is placed between two trees near Jerusalem.", "reasons": "Ka'b supplies this location."}, {"id": "7:8/q18/p5", "position": "A huge balance overwhelms David, and half a date of charity can fill one pan by God's pleasure.", "reasons": "Alusi relays this tradition as an illustration of divine valuation."}]}

{"id": "7:8/q20", "question": "What is the inward or moral scale?", "turns_on": "Which human faculties or ethical criteria a spiritual application treats as the pans, tongue, or weighted acts.", "positions": [{"id": "7:8/q20/p1", "position": "One weighs self, thoughts, and breaths by justice and truth, becoming humble or content with divine witnessing.", "reasons": "Sulami reports a spiritual instruction to weigh the self by justice and thoughts and breaths by truth."}, {"id": "7:8/q20/p2", "position": "Soul and spirit weigh obedience by scripture; heart and intellect weigh reward by promise and warning; gnosis weighs divine approval.", "reasons": "Sulami distinguishes the scales and calls flight and seeking the two pans of gnosis and secret."}, {"id": "7:8/q20/p3", "position": "The inner scale has justice for its tongue, sense and intellect for pans; lasting virtue and sincere intention give it weight.", "reasons": "Qashani applies it at the lesser resurrection, yielding the heart's paradise of divine attributes; temporary sensations, desire, and vice lack weight."}, {"id": "7:8/q20/p4", "position": "Reason, knowledge, and sound will function as balances for truth, lawful conduct, and felicity.", "reasons": "Tha'labi relays a moral interpretation distinguishing true and false, licit and illicit, and happiness and misery."}, {"id": "7:8/q20/p5", "position": "Different balances suit bodily, spiritual, secret, and hidden ethical qualities.", "reasons": "Bursawi relays the Najmi interpretation and the Prophetic saying that good character is heaviest because humans emulate God's qualities."}]}
{"id": "7:8/q21", "question": "How is physical heaviness itself explained?", "turns_on": "Whether heaviness is an additional attribute or reducible to constituent parts.", "positions": [{"id": "7:8/q21/p1", "position": "Heaviness is a distinct downward tendency of a heavy object.", "reasons": "Abu Hashim, reported by Jishumi, treats it as a positive attribute. {"id": "7:9/q01", "question": "What does the balance or weighing at Judgment signify?", "turns_on": "Whether the balance is a physical instrument, a figure for justice, or a measure of truth in acts; whether deeds have bodily weight and what the weighing demonstrates.", "positions": [{"id": "7:9/q01/p1", "position": "A real balance is set up and publicly weighs on Judgment Day.", "reasons": "Ibn Atiyya cites the visible balance in a Prophetic report and warns against abandoning the apparent sense; Ibn al-Jawzi cites hadith. {"id": "70:19/q02", "question": "What does halūʿ mean?", "turns_on": "Whether the term itself names the paired reactions, one reaction or desire, a deeper lack of restraint, or eager pursuit of perceived good; Ibn Ashur appeals to poetry to distinguish halʿ from distress.", "positions": [{"id": "70:19/q02/p1", "position": "It is a twofold disposition: intense distress or impatience at harm and greed or withholding when good comes.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan, al-Farra, Abu Ubayda, Tha'lab, Ibn Abbas, and many authors use 70:20-21 as God's explanation; reports vary between panic, despair, irritation, insufficient patience or gratitude, greed, and refusal to share. Al-Nahhas specifies poverty and withholding obligatory rights when wealthy; al-Kashshaf and al-Nasafi allow wealth or health versus poverty or illness; al-Qurtubi specifies God's due and people's share. Al-Farra derives the pattern from jazaʿ. Al-Kashshaf, Abu Hayyan, al-Samin, and al-Alusi cite a swift, light she-camel to explain rapid reactions; al-Qurtubi cites a poetic line for that usage. Al-Durr cites Bashr ibn Abi Hazim's poetry. Al-Wahidi records Amr ibn Ma'dikarib's line and al-Mubarrad's appeal to seeking refuge from panic in battle. The prophetic reports describe anxious greed and disabling cowardice among the worst traits. Ibn Ashur reports Tha'lab's explanation but objects that the two reactions do not entail one another as one lexical definition. Abu al-Aliya in al-Burhan and Ibn Abbas in al-Durr Full explicitly take God's following description as the answer to what haluʿ means. Bint al-Shati agrees with al-Farra and Tha'lab that the Quran explains it through panic at harm and withholding at good; al-Farra adds that one is readily distressed. Al-Samarra'i likewise reads 70:20-21 as defining it and reports al-Kashshaf's gloss of quick despair and quick withholding, with wealth and poverty as one account of good and harm."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p2", "position": "It means distress, fretfulness, agitation, grief, or impatience.", "reasons": "Al-Majaz appeals to the next verses for failure to endure. Al-Tabari transmits Ikrima, Ibn Zayd, and Qatada; al-Tha'labi also reports sorrow or grief from Qatada and Ibn Zayd. Al-Wahidi transmits al-Farra. Ibn Atiyya relates agitation to fears and desires; Ibn al-Jawzi includes Ibn Qutayba's intense distress; al-Durr cites Bashr ibn Abi Hazim for Arabic usage. Ibn Ashur says many linguists use distress but argues it is an effect rather than the trait itself, testing the distinction with Amr ibn Ma'dikarib's verse. Abu Hayyan glosses the related jazaʿ as fear and cites a poetic line. Al-Itqan reports the distressed and impatient gloss with Bishr ibn Abi Hazim's verse as evidence. Bint al-Shati reports Ibn Abbas's exchange with Nafi ibn al-Azraq, where he glosses the word as distressed and prone to lament and cites Bishr's line; she also reports lexicographers who narrow the sense to extreme distress, sometimes specifically panic and lack of patience at calamity."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p3", "position": "It means miserliness or stinginess.", "reasons": "Sa'id ibn Jubayr, al-Hasan, and al-Dahhak are among those reported with this gloss. Al-Qurtubi explains withholding God's due from received wealth. Ibn Ashur classifies this as an effect of the broader weakness of restraint."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p4", "position": "It means greed, covetousness, or voracious desire, sometimes specifically for what is unlawful.", "reasons": "Al-Hasan, Husayn, Ikrima, Mujahid, and Ibn Abbas are variously transmitted with the gloss; al-Dahhak describes someone never satiated, or never satisfied with amassed wealth. The al-Suddi report from Ibn Abbas and Ibn al-Jawzi's report specify unlawful objects. Ibn Ashur treats greed and hunger as effects of a broader trait."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p5", "position": "It is love of pleasure and flight from pain.", "reasons": "Ibn Kaysan and al-Asamm add the moral countercommand: give what one loves and patiently endure what one dislikes."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p6", "position": "It is restlessness as the soul follows desires and changes with possession or loss.", "reasons": "Sahl describes fluctuation with appetite. Ibn Ata describes contentment when possessing and resentment at loss, even of a small worldly gain; Bursevi repeats this. Abu al-Hasan al-Warraq adds cursing in affliction and supplication under trial."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p7", "position": "It means haste, swift agitation, or quickness.", "reasons": "Ata supplies the haste gloss, though al-Tha'labi's excerpt cuts off another gloss. Abu Muslim compares a fast, light she-camel. Ibn Ashur also lists haste among effects rather than the central trait. Bint al-Shati reports lexical uses of related forms for a quick-moving ostrich whose lightness makes it startle, as well as for a fast-moving she-camel."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p8", "position": "It means narrowness of heart.", "reasons": "This gloss is attributed to Muqatil by al-Tha'labi, al-Jishumi, and al-Baghawi."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p9", "position": "It is weak self-restraint before actual or anticipated pleasure or pain.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur prefers this broader trait. Amr ibn Ma'dikarib's line separately denies halʿ and jazaʿ, so he rejects treating them as synonyms; he says al-Marquzi's mild-versus-severe-grief explanation fails. Greed, irritation, miserliness, hunger, and cowardice are effects. The condition becomes apparent on perceiving benefit or harm."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p10", "position": "It is intense eagerness for perceived personal good.", "reasons": "Al-Tabatabai prefers eagerness; perceived harm frustrates it and causes panic, while perceived benefits prompt selfish retention. Children's pursuit of apparent good, resistance to sharing, later rational revision, and persistent appetite illustrate how it works."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p11", "position": "It means weakness.", "reasons": "Al-Mawardi attributes this gloss to Abu al-Ghiyath."}, {"id": "70:19/q02/p12", "position": "It expresses the ego's dark, impure attachment, producing cowardice and greed.", "reasons": "Al-Qashani interprets the distress and withholding of the following verses as manifestations of attachment to the ego's nature."}]}

{"id": "70:19/q04", "question": "How do the following descriptions of distress and withholding relate to halūʿ?", "turns_on": "Whether the next two clauses are a lexical definition of one compound trait or name distinct effects of a deeper trait.", "positions": [{"id": "70:19/q04/p1", "position": "They are explanatory clauses or descriptions that unpack the preceding word.", "reasons": "Al-Burhan says explanatory clauses are common in the Quran. Al-Itqan cites rhetoricians that such clauses remove ambiguity, and Abu al-Aliya applies this here. Ibn Jinni, quoted in al-Burhan and al-Itqan, says one should not pause before the explanatory clause because it completes its antecedent like a relative clause or adjective. Al-Qurtubi says jazuʿan and manuʿan are adjectives brought before the condition, or predicates of an implicit kana; many exegetes take God's following words as the clearest explanation of halūʿ. Abu al-Aliya in al-Burhan, Ibn Abbas in al-Durr Full, al-Farra as reported by Bint al-Shati, Bint al-Shati herself, and al-Samarra'i explicitly say the next verses explain or define haluʿ through the paired reactions."}, {"id": "70:19/q04/p2", "position": "The two distinct reactions are effects of a broader underlying trait, so they do not jointly define a single lexical sense.", "reasons": "Ibn Ashur rejects Tha'lab's loose equation: if two clauses defined one compound word, their different meanings would have to imply one another. {"id": "70:19/q11", "question": "How can the disposition be restrained or overcome?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "70:19/q11/p1", "position": "Steady prayer and the qualities of the exempt believers train patience, generosity, desire, and attention.", "reasons": "Al-Kashshaf distinguishes regularly performing prayer from guarding its ablution, time, pillars, sunna, manners, and protection against invalidating sins; the Prophet calls consistent work best even if little, and Aisha reports his practice was continuous. Al-Samarra'i says persistent attentive prayer treats panic and withholding by giving time and self to God despite worldly costs (62:11), while guarding chastity trains restraint against tempting opportunities (23:5-7). Study Quran says the eight qualities of 70:22-35 exempt their possessors. Al-Tabatabai says developed reason redirects eagerness toward real good, fear of sin, forgiveness, and patience under duty. Al-Samarra'i says giving to the poor (70:24-25) cures both reactions: the giver does not grieve over wealth leaving and does not withhold the needy person's share. He also says faith in Judgment and fear of punishment bring reassurance, patience under harm in hope of God's reward, and generosity in expectation of multiplied repayment (70:26-28)."}, {"id": "70:19/q11/p2", "position": "Accept God's decree and direct health and wealth toward gain in the Hereafter.", "reasons": "Study Quran reports al-Razi's advice to recognize that circumstances come from God and be content, and to spend health and wealth seeking the Hereafter rather than this life."}]}
{"id": "70:19/q12", "question": "What wisdom does al-Razi find in the created human body's capacity for speech?", "turns_on": "", "positions": [{"id": "70:19/q12/p1", "position": "The body and breathing serve the soul's pursuit of knowledge and right action, while articulated speech enables easy, precise communication.", "reasons": "Al-Razi says people need others to meet their needs and speech is easier than writing or gesture.
